hints: Focus on how many bonding pairs and lone pairs are on nitrogen in $\text{NH}_3$ compared to $\text{NH}_4^+$.
Ammonia has 3 N-H bonds plus 1 lone pair, while ammonium has 4 N-H bonds and no lone pair.
Remember that every single bond is a sigma bond, including the dative covalent bond formed when $\text{NH}_3$ becomes $\text{NH}_4^+$.
walkthrough:
**Count electron pairs on nitrogen**

Think of shape as decided by electron pairs, not just atoms. $\text{NH}_3$ has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair. $\text{NH}_4^+$ has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs.

$$\text{NH}_3: 3 \text{ bp} + 1 \text{ lp} \quad , \quad \text{NH}_4^+: 4 \text{ bp} + 0 \text{ lp}$$

**Predict the shapes**

A lone pair squeezes the bonds down, so 3 bp + 1 lp gives trigonal pyramidal. With 4 bp and no lone pair, all four directions are equal, giving regular tetrahedral.

$$\text{NH}_3 = \text{pyramidal}, \quad \text{NH}_4^+ = \text{regular tetrahedral}$$

**Identify the bond types**

All N-H bonds here are single bonds, and every single bond contains one $\sigma$ bond. The fourth bond in $\text{NH}_4^+$ is dative covalent, but once formed it is still just a $\sigma$ bond, with no $\pi$ bond present.

options.A: Correct. Ammonia is pyramidal due to 3 bonding pairs plus 1 lone pair, and ammonium is regular tetrahedral due to 4 bonding pairs. Both contain only single $\sigma$ bonds.
options.B: Shapes are right but bond type for ammonium is wrong. Students sometimes think the dative covalent bond must be different, but it is still a $\sigma$ bond, not a $\pi$ bond.
options.C: Shapes are swapped. A common trap is to forget the lone pair on ammonia, thinking 3 atoms must mean tetrahedral, and to forget that adding $\text{H}^+$ removes the lone pair to give tetrahedral ammonium.
options.D: Both shapes and the ammonia bond type are wrong. $\pi$ bonds only occur in multiple bonds, and both $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{NH}_4^+$ contain only single bonds.
